newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FEATURE-Argentina purges reviled police force.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Argentina purges reviled police force.

text.p: It is 6 a.m. in Buenos Aires' Constitucion railway station and a long-haired teen-ager on his way home from a nightclub has just been shot and killed by a drunk.
The killer takes refuge on a train and is surrounded by police. "Cool it, I'm a cop," he shouts, flashing a badge.

The Buenos Aires Province Police sergeant, who had been drinking after he was stood up by his girlfriend, took a passing dislike to 19-year-old Diego Aguilera. The 47,000 members of the force, which is larger even than the army, are under orders to carry their revolvers even while off duty.

The story is told by Maria del Carmen Verdu, a lawyer for pressure group Coordination Against Police and Institutional Violence (COREPI), set up to document illegal killings by police since democracy was restored in Argentina in 1983.

Amnesty International has documented "dozens of murders by police in circumstances indicating extra-judicial executions," and human rights lawyers at the Center for Legal and Social Studies list 153 fatal victims of police violence in Buenos Aires and greater Buenos Aires alone last year.

Crime by police has become so endemic it has spawned a new genre in journalism among crime reporters no longer able to distinguish the cops from the robbers. It is no surprise that opinion polls show more than 90 percent of Argentines have little or no faith in the police.
POLICEMAN A PRIME SUSPECT IN JOURNALIST MURDER
Carlos Dutil of the weekly news magazine Noticias has just written a book on the Buenos Aires Province Police, which has the worst reputation of the country's two dozen police forces.

In January Dutil's colleague, photographer Jose Luis Cabezas, was shot dead and his body burned to blackened bones. No one was surprised when four hoods who confessed to helping abduct him said they were hired by a Buenos Aires province policeman who is now the prime suspect in the murder.

The klling followed a bad 1996 for Argentina's largest security force, which far outnumbers the 31,000-strong Federal Police. Four officers were indicted for a 1994 anti-Jewish bomb attack that killed 86, entire drug and fraud squads were sent down for extortion and drugs, and newspapers were full of beatings, rapes, torture and murders by the boys in blue.

Provincial Gov. Eduardo Duhalde, who wants to succeed President Carlos Menem, once described his force as "the best police in the world." He now says: "When people see a squad car at night, rather than feeling protected they feel fear."

The province has purged 1,000 officers from the ranks this year and at least 100 more will follow, new Security Secretary Carlos Brown said. When he set up a police complaints hotline in July it could not cope with the influx of calls and collapsed in 48 hours; Brown concluded that the province's police problem exhibited "terminal characteristics."

One of his first jobs will be to review a police code drawn up by late Police Chief Ramon Camps, an infamous figure of the 1976-83 military juntas' "Dirty War" in which thousands of people, possibly tens of thousands, were killed.
BIG-TIME KILLER DREW UP POLICE CODE

This means Argentina's largest security force is being run on rules designed by a man convicted of 214 kidnaps, 120 torture cases, 32 murders, two rapes, two abortions provoked by torture, 18 robberies and 10 child kidnappings.
"We cannot permit that," Brown told Reuters. "We are a democracy now ... and they have absolutely no excuse."

Unlike the armed forces, purged after army revolts in the late 1980s, humbled by budget cuts and redeemed by a historic "mea culpa" in 1995, the police have gone largely untouched, "so the system keeps right on reproducing itself," Dutil said.

He partly blames the violence on the hard line on crime demanded by Duhalde and Menem, both of whom publicly support the death penalty for drug crimes. "When you know your police are born of military rule but you demand a hard hand, give them guns but don't train them, then tell them they're the best in the world, you're giving them a free hand and saying that's your security policy," Dutil said.

"And you must not forget the police's place in society's pecking order. In Argentina they have always been, at best, despised," he said. "That's why your average policeman is so close to the criminal element. In every family where there's a cop, there's also likely to be a robber."
That means violence goes hand-in-hand with corruption and police involvement in drugs, gambling and prostitution -- what Security Secretary Brown calls "the three scourges."
Verdu says top jobs at particularly lucrative precincts are auctioned off. In others pay and budgets are so tight they depend on bribes to pay for coffee and fuel for their cars.

Surprisingly, the police's best friend may be government human rights chief Alicia Pierini, a 56-year-old lawyer who once defended Montonero guerrilla leader Mario Firmenich. Now she organizes human rights training for police from Buenos Aires to Tierra del Fuego who she says are desperate to improve their appalling public image.

"They can't bear their reputation and being criticized even by their own kids," she told Reuters. "If society attacks the police ... and only thinks about how to put them in jail, what sort of police force will be have? Can we have a state without police?"
